title: "3. The density matrix as a feature"
order: 3
---

::: {.section-badges}
[Stage 5 fair comparison]{.badge-pill} [Hilbert → ρ → linear SVM]{.badge-pill} [10-fold × 10 CV + LOSO]{.badge-pill} [N = 28 pilot]{.badge-pill}
:::

::: {.callout-note}
**At this scale.** This is a pilot at N = 28. Under permutation testing, no cell — including density-matrix features — is significantly above chance at the conventional α = 0.05 threshold; the best cells sit at p ≈ 0.08. The "fair comparison" subsection at the end of this section runs density-matrix features against classical QEEG features under matched 2×2 design (feature set × model class) with subject-level leave-one-out and paired DeLong tests; that is the version a methods-sensitive reader should weight. Replication at N = 100 and on OpenNeuro ds004284 is the test that matters. Numbers in this section are reported for transparency about pilot-stage method development, not as established findings.
:::

The pivot in Section 2 ended on a question. What does a feature space of the right shape look like for this signal? Theta/beta ratio is one specific reduction of a much richer object. The classifier that survived cross-validation was reading off relative beta power across the back of the head, but the deeper observation is that the cleaned EEG carries cross-channel and cross-frequency structure the textbook power-and-coherence menu collapses into pairwise scalars. The density matrix is the smallest object I know that keeps that structure intact.

The construction is short. For each band $b$ in $\{\delta, \theta, \alpha, \beta\}$, zero-phase Butterworth bandpass each of the fifteen channels, take the Hilbert transform of each, and stack them at every time point into a complex column vector $\psi(t) \in \mathbb{C}^{15}$. Normalize $\psi(t)$ to unit length, take the outer product against itself, and average over all kept time samples across all epochs:

$$ \rho_b \;=\; \frac{1}{T} \sum_t \frac{\psi(t)\,\psi(t)^{\dagger}}{\|\psi(t)\|^2} $$

The result is a Hermitian, positive semi-definite, trace-one $15 \times 15$ complex matrix. It is a density matrix in the formal quantum-mechanical sense, even though every step of the construction is classical signal processing. Across twenty-eight children and four bands, max trace error is $4 \times 10^{-16}$ and min eigenvalue stays above $-7 \times 10^{-17}$, both within float64 round-off. Cauchy-Schwarz holds throughout.

Hover any cell to read the channel pair, $|\rho_{ij}|$, and the off-diagonal phase $\arg(\rho_{ij})$ in radians. Diagonal entries are channel occupation probabilities; off-diagonal entries carry cross-channel covariance and phase relationships that pairwise coherence and band power summaries throw away. The alpha band's central-parietal block is consistent with the SHAP top-three from Section 2 (Pz, P3, O1).
:::

For each subject and band, I flatten the matrix into a real feature vector. Fifteen real diagonals plus the real and imaginary parts of the 105 strict upper-triangle entries gives 225 reals per band, 900 features in total at $N = 15$. The $(\mathrm{Re}, \mathrm{Im})$ decomposition is mathematically equivalent to magnitude and phase but avoids the cyclic-angle pathology that breaks linear classifiers on phase. A linear SVM with top-ten ANOVA feature selection inside each fold runs under repeated stratified 10-fold cross-validation, ten repeats, fixed seed, the same fold indices reused for every model on every feature set. On the same twenty-eight children, that classifier reaches a mean balanced accuracy of [0.657]{.num-chip} and a mean ROC AUC of [0.780]{.num-chip}.

For comparison, I ran the same children through the standard QEEG menu under the same cross-validation: absolute and relative band power, frontal alpha asymmetry, theta/beta ratio, fronto-parietal coherence, alpha reactivity, and band-limited covariance, 622 features in total. The best per-fold classifier on that feature set is a Random Forest at [0.618]{.num-chip} mean balanced accuracy, [0.615]{.num-chip} ROC AUC. On the same data, the density-matrix features pull the per-fold mean AUC from 0.615 to 0.780.

That headline contrast, however, was the first version of this section and put DM features under one model class (linear SVM) against classical features under a different model class (shallow Random Forest). The original Stage 5 script also used per-fold bootstrap CIs (resampling 100 folds, n_subjects = 28) and a per-fold Wilcoxon test that treated correlated folds as independent — both produce CIs and p-values that are too tight at small N. The honest re-run is in the "Fair comparison" subsection at the end of this section; it leaves the numerical gap intact under the matched-SVM comparison but reveals that the DM-vs-classical contrast is sensitive to the classical-side model choice (it does not survive under matched RF), and that the subject-level 95% CIs on AUC are 2-3× wider than originally reported and do overlap.

The density matrix also appears in supervised quantum machine learning, but as a fidelity kernel rather than a feature. By Schuld's 2021 result on the kernel-equivalence of supervised quantum models [@schuld2021], a quantum-kernel SVM with feature map $|\psi(x)\rangle$ computes pairwise similarities as squared overlaps:

$$ K_Q(x, y) \;=\; |\langle\psi(x)|\psi(y)\rangle|^2 \;=\; \mathrm{Tr}(\rho_x \rho_y) $$

```{=html}
<details class="equation-explain">
  <summary>Read this equation, term by term</summary>
  <dl>
    <dt>K<sub>Q</sub>(x, y)</dt>
    <dd>The quantum-fidelity kernel: a single non-negative number measuring how similar inputs <em>x</em> and <em>y</em> are after the encoding circuit lifts them into Hilbert space.</dd>
    <dt>|ψ(x)⟩, |ψ(y)⟩</dt>
    <dd>The two inputs encoded as quantum state vectors. The bra-ket symbols are physics shorthand for column vectors and their conjugate transposes.</dd>
    <dt>⟨ψ(x) | ψ(y)⟩</dt>
    <dd>The complex inner product. Close to one when the two encoded states overlap; close to zero when they are orthogonal.</dd>
    <dt>| · |<sup>2</sup></dt>
    <dd>Squared magnitude. Maps the complex inner product back to a real, non-negative similarity.</dd>
    <dt>Tr(ρ<sub>x</sub> ρ<sub>y</sub>)</dt>
    <dd>The Hilbert-Schmidt inner product on density matrices. Schuld (2021) showed this equals the squared overlap above, so the kernel can be computed from the density matrices alone, without ever evaluating the encoding circuit.</dd>
  </dl>
</details>
```

If the quantum kernel and the explicit density-matrix features were equivalent on this data, an SVM with a precomputed Hilbert-Schmidt kernel $K(s, t) = \frac{1}{B}\sum_b \mathrm{Tr}(\rho_b^s \rho_b^t)$ should land in the same neighbourhood as a parameterised quantum-circuit kernel on quantum-inspired summary features (QEPP, von Neumann entropy, and related terms from the pipeline's Stage 5). On this cohort, under matched cross-validation, the two kernels do not converge. The Hilbert-Schmidt SVM reaches mean balanced accuracy 0.540, AUC 0.395. The parameterised quantum kernel on the Stage 5 features reaches 0.495 and 0.525. The paired Wilcoxon difference between the two kernels is +0.045 with $p = 0.44$, not distinguishable from zero.

::: {.figure-caption}
**Figure 5 (updated).** Subject-level leave-one-out ROC AUC across six classifiers under the same matched 10-fold × 10 cross-validation, $N = 28$. Whiskers on the four direct-feature bars are 95% subject-bootstrap CIs over 10 000 resamples of subjects (replacing the earlier per-fold bootstrap which was too tight at this N). The two kernel proxies (red) are mean only; their per-fold AUCs were not retained by the original Stage 5 / Hilbert-Schmidt evaluators and the rerun is queued. The classical-feature linear SVM (teal, AUC = 0.32) sits below chance — consistent with high-dimensional overfitting on 622 features under top-10 ANOVA selection at $N = 28$ — and sets a low bar. Under matched linear-SVM, density-matrix features beat classical features substantially (DeLong paired test on subject-level AUC, $p = 0.001$). Under matched Random Forest, the gap is small and not significant (DeLong $p = 0.51$). The original headline contrast (DM-SVM vs Classical-RF) shows ΔAUC = +0.17 with DeLong $p = 0.26$ — the gap survives the rerun, the statistical significance does not. The dashed vertical rule marks chance performance.
:::

The two kernels reach below the chance line for different reasons, and the right reading needs both. The parameterised quantum-circuit kernel runs on the Stage 5 quantum-inspired summary features, which are first compressed through PCA to six dimensions and rescaled to $[0, \pi]$ before encoding; none of those steps preserve the off-diagonal complex structure that the explicit density matrix exposes, so the QSVM is operating on a lossy projection. The Hilbert-Schmidt kernel, by contrast, reads $\rho$ directly without PCA. At $N = 28$ with the binarised executive-function outcome the 95% bootstrap CI on AUC = 0.395 overlaps the 0.5 chance line, so whether that score reflects a structured anti-alignment between the cohort-mean fidelity geometry and the median split or sub-sample variance at this $N$ is exactly what the ds004284 replication is designed to test. What the explicit-feature result shows is more limited and more defensible: on this cohort and at this scale, the entries of $\rho$ carry information that survives explicit feature extraction in a way the similarity-matrix view does not.

```{=html}
<script>
(function () {
  d3.json("../assets/kernel_mds_data.json").then(function (data) {
    var COLORS = { "0": "#b73e3e", "1": "#2c5f4f", "-1": "#9aa3b3" };
    var LABELS = data.group_labels;

    function buildTraces(embKey) {
      var emb = data.embeddings[embKey];
      var groups = {};
      data.subjects.forEach(function (s, idx) {
        var g = String(data.groups[idx]);
        if (!groups[g]) groups[g] = { name: LABELS[g] || ("Group " + g),
                                        color: COLORS[g] || "#9aa3b3",
                                        x: [], y: [], text: [] };
        groups[g].x.push(emb.x[idx]);
        groups[g].y.push(emb.y[idx]);
        groups[g].text.push(s);
      });
      return Object.keys(groups).map(function (k) {
        var g = groups[k];
        return {
          type: "scatter", mode: "markers",
          name: g.name,
          x: g.x, y: g.y, text: g.text,
          hovertemplate: "<b>%{text}</b><br>" + g.name + "<extra></extra>",
          marker: {
            size: 11, color: g.color, opacity: 0.86,
            line: { width: 1.2, color: "#fbf9f4" }
          }
        };
      });
    }

    var layout = {
      autosize: true, height: 380,
      margin: { l: 44, r: 24, t: 20, b: 40 },
      paper_bgcolor: "#fbf9f4", plot_bgcolor: "#fbf9f4",
      font: { family: "IBM Plex Sans, sans-serif", size: 11, color: "#3a4055" },
      xaxis: { title: { text: "MDS dimension 1", standoff: 10 },
                zeroline: true, zerolinecolor: "rgba(110,127,153,0.35)",
                gridcolor: "rgba(110,127,153,0.18)" },
      yaxis: { title: { text: "MDS dimension 2", standoff: 10 },
                zeroline: true, zerolinecolor: "rgba(110,127,153,0.35)",
                gridcolor: "rgba(110,127,153,0.18)",
                scaleanchor: "x", scaleratio: 1 },
      legend: { orientation: "h", x: 0, y: 1.12, xanchor: "left",
                 bgcolor: "rgba(0,0,0,0)" },
      hoverlabel: { bgcolor: "#fbf9f4",
                     font: { family: "IBM Plex Sans, sans-serif", size: 11,
                              color: "#1f1f1f" },
                     bordercolor: "rgba(107, 79, 142, 0.4)" }
    };
    var config = { displayModeBar: false, responsive: true };

    Plotly.newPlot("kernel-mds-plot", buildTraces("flat_features"),
                    layout, config);

    var btns = document.querySelectorAll(".kernel-mds-btn");
    btns.forEach(function (btn) {
      btn.addEventListener("click", function () {
        btns.forEach(function (b) { b.classList.remove("is-active"); });
        btn.classList.add("is-active");
        Plotly.react("kernel-mds-plot", buildTraces(btn.dataset.emb),
                      layout, config);
      });
    });
  }).catch(function (err) {
    var n = document.getElementById("kernel-mds-plot");
    if (n) n.innerHTML =
      '<p style="color:#b73e3e;font-family:IBM Plex Sans,sans-serif;font-size:0.9em">' +
      'Failed to load kernel-MDS data: ' + err.message + '</p>';
  });
})();
</script>
```

::: {.figure-caption}
**Figure 6.** Two-dimensional metric-MDS embedding of the 28 subjects under each kernel, coloured by the median split on Global Executive Function. The linear-kernel embedding on the flat density-matrix features (after standardisation), shown first, separates the two groups more cleanly; clicking through to the Hilbert-Schmidt embedding shows substantial overlap between groups under the fidelity geometry. The geometry is the visualisation of the AUC contrast in Figure 5.
:::

```{=html}
<iframe class="d3-interactive cv-slider-frame"
        src="../interactive/cv_slider_shap.html"
        title="Per-fold balanced accuracy and top-feature contributions for classical versus density-matrix features under matched 10-fold cross-validation"
        loading="lazy"
        height="640">
</iframe>
```

::: {.figure-caption}
**Figure 7 (interactive).** Per-fold balanced accuracy under the same matched 10-fold × 10-repeats split used for Figure 5, with each fold's score averaged across the ten repeats. Drag the slider or hover any bar to see the top features the classifier relied on at that fold. Classical features are top-three relative beta power at posterior channels (Pz, P3, O1) every fold; the structured-feature panel surfaces a mixture of $\rho_{ii}$ diagonals and off-diagonal real / imaginary parts that varies across folds, which is the small-sample noise that underwrites the per-fold variance you can see in the bar heights.
:::

What the data shows, end to end, under matched cross-validation and subject-level leave-one-out resampling at $N = 28$: a linear classifier on the 900 entries of $\rho$ reaches LOSO AUC $0.785$ (95% subject-bootstrap CI $[0.58, 0.95]$), against $0.617$ ($[0.39, 0.83]$) for the best classical-QEEG classifier (Random Forest on 622 spectral and coherence features). The matched-SVM contrast is robust (DeLong paired test on subject-level AUC, $p = 0.001$); the matched-RF contrast is not ($p = 0.51$); the original cross-model contrast (DM-SVM vs Classical-RF) sits between them with $p = 0.26$. Two parallel kernel routes to the same density matrix, one through the Hilbert-Schmidt inner product and one through a parameterised circuit, both underperform the direct features. The signal lives in the entries of $\rho$, and the right reading at this scale is: **the density-matrix representation appears to compress signal more usefully than the conventional QEEG menu, but the strength of that claim is model-class-dependent and the CIs are wide enough that the matched-RF comparison should be treated as a tie until N = 100.** The kernels are one specific way of accessing the same information that, at this scale and on these features, throws information away.

### Fair comparison summary (replication-ready)

For the methodologically sensitive reader who skipped the rest of this section: the 2×2 design (feature set × model class) under matched 10-fold × 10 CV with leave-one-subject-out probabilities and paired subject-level DeLong tests is the inference to weight. Results:

| Feature set | Model | LOSO AUC [95% subject-bootstrap CI] | LOSO BAcc [CI] | Permutation $p$ vs chance |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Density matrix | Linear SVM | 0.785 [0.58, 0.95] | 0.752 [0.59, 0.90] | 0.078 |
| Density matrix | Shallow RF | 0.714 [0.49, 0.90] | 0.537 [0.35, 0.72] | 0.098 |
| Classical QEEG | Linear SVM | 0.320 [0.11, 0.54] | 0.428 [0.25, 0.61] | 0.569 |
| Classical QEEG | Shallow RF | 0.617 [0.39, 0.83] | 0.642 [0.46, 0.82] | 0.118 |

Paired DeLong (subject-level AUC): DM-SVM vs Classical-SVM $p = 0.001$ · DM-RF vs Classical-RF $p = 0.51$ · DM-SVM vs Classical-RF (original portfolio comparison) $p = 0.26$. No cell is significantly above chance at the conventional $α = 0.05$ threshold under permutation testing — the best cells sit at $p ≈ 0.08$.

The honest one-liner: under matched linear SVM, density-matrix features carry information classical features do not; under matched RF, the contrast is not detectable at $N = 28$. The full numerical artifact is in [`results/stage5_fair_comparison.json`](https://github.com/Yazidryuichi/biomarker-iium-pipeline/blob/main/results/stage5_fair_comparison.json) of the pipeline repo.

::: {.notation-glossary}
Notation

| Symbol | Meaning |
|---|---|
| $\rho_b$ | density matrix at frequency band $b \in \{\delta, \theta, \alpha, \beta\}$, Hermitian positive semi-definite, trace one |
| $\psi(t)$ | complex multichannel analytic signal at time $t$, vector in $\mathbb{C}^{15}$ |
| $\psi(t)^{\dagger}$ | conjugate transpose of $\psi(t)$ |
| $K_Q(x, y)$ | quantum-fidelity kernel: squared overlap of embedded states |
| $\mathrm{Tr}(\rho_x \rho_y)$ | Hilbert-Schmidt inner product of two density matrices |
| $p$ | paired Wilcoxon two-sided p-value comparing matched per-fold accuracies |
:::
